These gains contrasted with sobering comments on fatalities, higher costs, and lingering uncertainty around U.S. incentives and global growth.

Record Group Revenue and EBITDA Expansion

Six-month group revenue came in just under ZAR 90 billion, a 64% jump year-on-year, reflecting broad-based strength across commodities and regions. Adjusted EBITDA surged 111% to ZAR 31.8 billion, delivering a 35% margin, while profit climbed 581%, underscoring powerful operational leverage in the current price environment.

Robust Cash Generation and Balance Sheet Strength

Commodity Price Tailwinds Across Key Markets

Results were strongly supported by higher commodity prices, with both South African and U.S. PGM baskets up about 70% year-on-year and local gold prices up 35%. Australian zinc also contributed, with a 25% price increase lifting profitability at the Century operation despite its near-end-of-life status.

South African PGM: Solid Delivery and Strong Margins

South African PGM production of 790,000 4E ounces matched guidance even as volumes were 2% lower year-on-year. Adjusted EBITDA from these assets rose to ZAR 19.2 billion, up 302%, and delivered a 44% all-in sustaining cost margin and 45% EBITDA margin, supported by higher basket prices and chrome byproduct credits.

PGM Cash Flow and Chrome’s Growing Role

Notional free cash flow from South African PGMs reached ZAR 10.4 billion, a ZAR 9.9 billion improvement year-on-year and a 54% conversion from EBITDA. Chrome contributed ZAR 1.1 billion in operating profit, and management expects a larger impact as UG2 feed is prioritized, even though chrome production dipped 18% after the planned closure of the BTT concentrator.

Record Earnings from South African Gold

South African gold sold rose 5% while the average gold price climbed 35%, driving adjusted EBITDA to a record ZAR 9 billion, up 87% year-on-year and yielding a 39% margin. Notional free cash flow of ZAR 3.9 billion reflected a 267% increase in cash generation, highlighting the earnings power of the gold segment in the current price cycle.

Surface Gold and DRDGOLD’s Performance

Surface gold output grew 13% to 105,000 ounces and now accounts for 36% of the South African gold mix, diversifying the production base. DRDGOLD produced 2.5 tonnes of gold with a 10% yield improvement, while Cooke’s production increased 11% on third-party material, bolstering overall surface contributions.

Burnstone Project: Long-Life, High-Return Gold

The Board approved the Burnstone project, envisioned to deliver roughly 130,000 ounces of gold per year at steady state over a 25-year life. With total project capital of around ZAR 6.2 billion, it carries a net present value of ZAR 19.2 billion and an internal rate of return of 36%, supported by existing shaft and surface infrastructure and a modest ZAR 98 million capital allocation in 2026.

Mount Lyell: Copper-Gold Growth in Tasmania

Mount Lyell, a copper-gold project in Tasmania, also received Board approval with total capital to production of about USD 340 million and a net present value of roughly USD 550 million. The 23-year project is expected to support around 300 steady-state jobs and deliver long-term copper and gold output, further diversifying Sibanye-Stillwater’s commodity and geographic exposure.

Dividend at Upper End of Payout Policy

The Board declared an interim dividend of ZAR 5.7 billion, or ZAR 2.01 per share, placing the payout at the upper end of the 25% to 35% normalized earnings policy range. The annualized dividend yield sits near 8% with a trailing 12-month yield of 6.6%, though management noted the policy is slightly below peers and is unlikely to rise materially until gross debt is cut by half.

U.S. PGM: Mechanization Progress Amid EBITDA Pressure

U.S. PGM production of 138,000 ounces of palladium and platinum was in line with guidance, and mechanized bolting trials at Stillwater East, along with operating-model work, advanced as planned. However, adjusted EBITDA dropped 56% to USD 66 million, with all-in sustaining costs up 12% to USD 1,347 per ounce, partly due to investment in mechanization and a tough comparison versus last year’s large Section 45X tax credit.

Improved U.S. Cash Performance Despite Investment

Notional free cash flow from U.S. PGMs remained negative at USD 28 million but represented a 52% reduction in cash outflow year-to-date. Higher palladium and platinum prices helped, while cash was deliberately deployed to fund mechanization, which management sees as critical to achieving a sustainable cost base.

Recycling Business: Scale and Margin Expansion

The recycling segment posted a 13% adjusted EBITDA margin, generating USD 164 million in adjusted EBITDA and USD 103 million in cash, a 63% conversion rate. Precious metals production jumped 142% year-on-year to about 2.8 million gold-equivalent ounces, underscoring the growing scale and strategic importance of this lower-capex, high-cash-flow business.

Century Zinc: Strong Cash, Limited Life

Century produced 45 kilotonnes of payable zinc, in line with guidance, and delivered USD 55 million of adjusted EBITDA, up 54% year-on-year, with notional free cash flow of USD 41 million, up 86%. Yet management stressed Century is nearing end of life, with an estimated 12 to 18 months of mining left and costs 23% higher year-on-year at USD 2,162 per tonne.

Keliber Lithium: Mining Progress, Refinery Decision Pending

At Keliber, mining is fully underway with 218 kilotonnes extracted and 186 kilotonnes added to the strategic stockpile, exceeding milestones and meeting targeted run rates. Concentrator commissioning is in progress and capital spending of EUR 719 million remains on plan against a EUR 783 million budget, but the decision to start the refinery still depends on concentrator performance and lithium market conditions.

Organic Growth Pipeline and Capital Discipline

The approved organic growth pipeline includes Thembelani, Siphumelele, Western Limb Tailings Retreatment, Burnstone and Mount Lyell, which collectively underpin production over the next five years. Management emphasized disciplined sequencing based on returns, affordability, readiness and strategic fit, even as operating-model changes across a multi-acquisition portfolio take longer than initially expected.

Renewable Energy and Water Independence Initiatives

Sibanye-Stillwater already has more than 165 megawatts of renewable energy in operation and expects this to exceed 835 megawatts by 2028, potentially saving over ZAR 1 billion in energy costs and bringing about half of power needs under its control. Water independence is improving, with South African gold operations at 95% and PGM operations at 42%, and plans to lift PGM water independence to 90% by 2028.

Safety Metrics Improve but Fatalities Persist

Safety indicators continue to trend downward, and management said performance compares favorably to both the company’s history and peers, noting Driefontein’s year without a fatal incident. However, three colleagues were lost to safety incidents and three to crime-related events in the quarter, which the company described as preventable challenges that remain a central focus.

Operational Headwinds in Gold and PGM Segments

South African PGM production was 2% lower year-on-year and all-in sustaining costs rose 10% to ZAR 26,252 per 4E ounce, driven by royalties, inflation and consumables despite chrome credits. South African gold output slipped 2% to 294,000 ounces, with underground volumes down 9% and costs higher due to shaft maintenance, winder upgrades, reserve development, water pumping, plant upgrades and double handling.

Kloof and Beatrix: Seismic and Infrastructure Challenges

Kloof 7 was closed and the broader Kloof operation rebased to reduce exposure to highly seismic ground, limiting access to some higher-grade areas but improving risk management. At Beatrix, seismic damage to footwall infrastructure cut off high-grade zones, although plant recoveries are now improving after maintenance intervention, suggesting gradual operational normalization.

Labor Negotiations and Mechanization Execution Risk

Two union labor agreements covering Stillwater and East Boulder remain under negotiation, complicated by the mechanization program’s impact on work practices, equipment use and team-based incentives. Management warned the mechanization process is multi-year and depends on workforce adoption and supervisory capability, adding that capital will not be heavily committed to future areas if targeted cost levels cannot be achieved.

Macroeconomic and Lithium Market Uncertainty

Management flagged macro and geopolitical risks, including conflict in the Middle East, weaker global growth forecasts and trade disruptions that could weigh on investment and industrial demand. Battery-grade lithium hydroxide prices fell 9% in the quarter and are expected to ease further as new supply arrives, although management does not foresee prices dropping below 2025 levels.

Section 45X Timing and Portfolio Simplification Delays

The U.S. tax authority has begun reviewing the 2023 return linked to the Section 45X credit and requested additional information and a potential site visit, leaving cash timing uncertain. Separately, management acknowledged that reshaping a portfolio built through multiple acquisitions is taking longer than anticipated, and that several simplification initiatives have not yet reached announcement stage.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Strategic Priorities

Management said the company remains on track to meet operational and financial guidance, with South African PGM output at 790,000 4E ounces and second-half costs set to rise but stay within the guided range. Century’s costs sit at the lower end of guidance, gold unit cost guidance has been lifted, lithium prices are expected to soften modestly, Stillwater is targeting USD 1,000 per ounce by 2028, and Burnstone and Mount Lyell are being developed under defined capital and life-of-mine frameworks, all while management works to reduce gross debt by 50% over two to three years within a firm dividend policy.

Sibanye-Stillwater’s call painted a picture of a miner enjoying a powerful earnings and cash upswing, yet acutely aware of safety, cost and macro risks. For investors, the combination of strong current returns, disciplined capital deployment and clear balance-sheet priorities, tempered by execution and market uncertainties, frames a compelling but not risk-free long-term story.

NextAR Hip entered limited release in the U.S. and Australia, while the Infinity triple-tapered stem moved to full rollout and gained traction in the U.S. and Japan, providing fresh catalysts for future volumes.

Knee Business Powered by Kinematic Alignment Strategy

The knee segment grew almost 11%, driven by Medacta’s focus on Kinematic Alignment and the GMK SpheriKA implant. Management said GMK SpheriKA is rapidly becoming its most important knee product, with segment growth running more than twice the market, underlining strong surgeon adoption of the alignment concept.

Extremities Surge With New Shoulder and Sports Medicine Tools

Extremities delivered standout performance, rising almost 16% and more than double market growth. The company rolled out revision shoulder arthroplasty in the U.S., began international expansion, and introduced the AI-based MyShoulder Planner, alongside Secure-Fix, an all-inside meniscal repair system that is expected to be a key driver in knee sports medicine.

Spine Technology Adoption and Shift to a More Profitable Model

In spine, enabling technology now accounts for roughly 50% of U.S. revenues, reflecting growing adoption of technology-supported procedures. Medacta is pivoting to a more direct and more exclusive agent model in the U.S., while spine profitability has moved from breakeven to positive, though still around a third of the margin of the core joint business.

India Approval Opens a New High-Growth Market

Medacta secured approval for its knee products in India just before the call and plans to begin shipping in September. Management sees India as a market with around EUR 100 million current potential and growth above 15%, albeit at low European pricing levels, adding a sizable emerging-market growth leg to the story.

U.S. Recovery Efforts and New Product Momentum

In the U.S., the company reported re-acceleration in hips tied to the triple-tapered stem, continued solid knee growth, and good traction from the new Monoblock shoulder stem. Medacta expects reduced spine dilution and believes base-customer attrition should ease thanks to a growing pipeline of new surgeons and accounts.

Ongoing Investment in Capacity and U.S. Infrastructure

CapEx reached EUR 74 million in H1, including EUR 42 million for instruments, EUR 22 million for tangible assets, EUR 8 million for R&D, and EUR 2 million for other items. Tangible investments focus on expanding production capacity, land, and buildings, aligning with plans for future manufacturing scale and staffing growth.

New U.S. Headquarters and Manufacturing Expansion in Tennessee

To support its accelerating U.S. development, Medacta acquired a large site in Tennessee for new headquarters and domestic manufacturing. This move should shorten supply chains and deepen local presence in the company’s most strategically important market, potentially boosting competitiveness and responsiveness to customers over time.

In-House Innovation Favored Over Large M&A

Management reiterated its preference for internal development, saying it delivers better returns on capital than big-ticket acquisitions. Medacta is building its own spine technology and robotics platform at a fraction of the cost of a peer’s large spine deal, while remaining open to smaller sports medicine and niche opportunities that fit its strategy.

Cost Discipline Helps Offset Gross Margin Erosion

Although costs had initially been set for higher anticipated growth, the company has since aligned spending with actual revenue trends. Management emphasized its ability to adjust operating expenses, noting that careful cost control partially offset the impact of gross margin erosion and helped preserve profitability.

Gross Margin Hit by FX, Pricing, and Mix Effects

Gross profit rose to EUR 240 million from EUR 233 million, but the margin dropped to 65.2% from 68.3%, a roughly 3-point decline. The fall was attributed to a 1.3% adverse FX impact, about 0.5% price erosion, and around 1.3% from geographic and product mix, including lower U.S. sales, higher sports medicine volumes, and a higher D&A ratio.

EBITDA Margin Pressure Reflects Limited Leverage

At constant currency, adjusted EBITDA margin slipped 0.9 percentage points from the prior semester once FX effects are stripped out. Management cited gross profit erosion as the main driver, with only modest operating leverage from higher volumes and cost discipline, signaling that margin expansion remains a work in progress.

Reported Earnings and Cash Flow Weaken, Leverage Ticks Up

Operating cash flow fell to about EUR 56 million from EUR 73 million, as EBITDA softness and higher working capital needs weighed on cash generation. Investing outflows of EUR 74 million produced negative free cash flow of EUR 18.6 million, and net debt leverage rose to 1.2x adjusted EBITDA from 0.9x at year-end, though still at conservative levels.

U.S. Market Slows, Customer Attrition and Spanish Strikes Bite

Management estimated U.S. market growth at only around 3% versus expected 5%–5.5%, dampening North American momentum. Base attrition among existing U.S. customers and surgeon shifts toward ambulatory centers hurt volumes, while public-sector strikes in Spain left that market down nearly 20%, even as Medacta’s Spanish unit still grew.

Spine and Sports Medicine Still Dilutive to Group Margins

Spine grew 4.5%, a subdued pace as Medacta transitions to a more profitable model focused on specialty products and technology-enabled sales. Sports medicine remains loss-making as the company invests in sales-force expansion and product development, and management flagged both spine and sports medicine as segments that must scale to reduce EBITDA dilution.

External Transportation Costs Add to Margin Headwinds

Fuel surcharges on external transportation have pushed up variable logistics costs, providing another drag on margins that management says is largely outside its control. Elevated fuel prices exacerbate cost pressure at a time when FX, pricing, and mix are already weighing on profitability, limiting near-term relief for gross margins.

Instrument Deployment Drives Higher D&A in a Softer Top Line

The D&A ratio increased because the company had placed a similar level of instruments into the market despite lower-than-expected revenues. These instruments were originally deployed for a stronger growth scenario, and management signaled that it may pull back some incremental instruments in the second half to ease the burden.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Market Context

Medacta reaffirmed its 2026 outlook for 10%–14% revenue growth and around 50 basis points of adjusted EBITDA margin expansion in constant currency, as well as midterm revenue CAGR of 12%–15% with gradual EBITDA improvement. Management said hitting the midpoint remains possible but more likely slightly below, noting that even 10%–12% growth would be nearly three times current market rates.

Medacta’s earnings call ultimately balanced strong growth and strategic progress against margin and cash-flow challenges. The company continues to outpace the market, backed by innovation, geographic diversification, and capacity expansion, while openly acknowledging pressure points in the U.S., spine, and sports medicine. For investors, the story remains one of above-market growth with a clear focus on improving profitability.

Fourth-Quarter EBITDA Surge

Bengalla’s Strong Operational Finish

Bengalla recorded raw coal output of 3.0 million tonnes in the quarter, up 16% on the previous period, with saleable coal at 2.3 million tonnes, up 8%. The mine hit targeted raw production of 13.4 million tonnes on a 100% basis, capping off a strong quarter that helped drive group performance.

Bengalla Volumes Exceed Full-Year Guidance

Over FY2026, Bengalla delivered 8.2 million tonnes of saleable coal and coal sales, surpassing its guidance range. The outperformance followed a recovery from severe Hunter region weather late in FY2025, highlighting the mine’s resilience and operational flexibility after disruption.

Bengalla Costs at Guidance Floor

Bengalla’s FY2026 FOB cash cost came in at $81.30 per sales tonne, at the lower end of the $81 to $89 guidance range. Achieving cost performance at the guidance floor in an inflationary environment underscores solid cost discipline and supports margins even as prices and demand fluctuate.

New Acland Ramp-Up Continues

New Acland Sales Above Guidance

Coal sales from New Acland reached 3.6 million tonnes in FY2026, exceeding guidance. Management said increased spot rail capacity during the year supported the stronger sales outcome, although they noted that logistics constraints remain an operating risk.

Advancing New Acland Growth Plans

The operation is ramping toward a 5 million tonnes per annum target, with access to the Manning Vale West pit scheduled for the second half of calendar 2026. First coal is expected shortly after, positioning New Acland as a growing contributor to group volumes over the medium term.

Low Strip Ratios Underpin Mine Economics

Bengalla’s strip ratio was about 4 in the quarter, and management expects it to stay in the 4s on average for the mine life. New Acland is also expected to average around a 4 strip ratio, supporting efficient waste movement and favourable long‑run operating economics.

Flexible Wash Strategy Protects Margins

Management highlighted an upgraded wash‑plant that allows switching between high‑ash and low‑ash coal, depending on market discounts. This flexible wash strategy aims to maximize profitability by tailoring product quality to prevailing demand and pricing conditions.

Optimizing Capital Expenditure

The group has deferred some sustaining capital via overhaul management, asset productivity initiatives and careful maintenance planning. Management stressed a focus on minimizing capex where possible while balancing the risk of unplanned breakdowns against equipment reliability needs.

Lower Capital Needs After Key Projects

Around $130 million has been earmarked to complete the Manning Vale West pit, including road realignment and fleet spending. Once this and additional Bengalla investment are finished, management expects capital requirements to moderate even as production continues to grow.

Shareholder Returns Backed by Cash and Franking

Management noted that cash balances are materially above the desired long‑term level and highlighted a significant franking account balance. They indicated that shareholders should continue to see rewards, pointing to the expectation of a reasonable dividend supported by strong cash flows.

Malabar Ramp-Up and Portfolio Optionality

At Malabar, the Maxwell Mine’s longwall is operating and productivity is expected to keep ramping up. Management said the operation should become cash generative in the near future, while newly acquired Mount Arthur tenements add optionality for longer‑term portfolio development.

Emerging Malabar Infrastructure Opportunities

Management flagged potential data‑center and battery‑related infrastructure opportunities tied to Malabar. Larger investment decisions remain ahead, with the immediate focus on fully ramping the Maxwell Mine before committing to any significant new capital in these adjacent areas.

Supportive Thermal Coal Market Backdrop

Ongoing conflict in the Middle East is expected to sustain volatility in energy markets, supporting thermal coal as a reliable baseload power source. Management suggested that continued supply concerns underpin demand for coal generation, benefiting the pricing environment for New Hope’s products.

Strengthened Safety Controls and Engagement

In response to a rise in high‑potential and serious events across the industry, the group implemented safety pauses and increased frontline engagement. Targeted reviews and verification of critical controls were undertaken, with fatal and serious‑harm risk management reaffirmed as a top priority.

Organic Growth as Core Strategy

Management reiterated that strategic focus remains on organic growth across existing assets rather than major external deals. They said no external opportunity currently fits the portfolio, suggesting capital will stay directed toward internal projects with clearer risk‑return profiles.

Rising High-Potential Event Frequency

While the total recordable injury frequency rate fell to 3.89, down 12% from the prior quarter, high‑potential event frequency worsened from 1.21 to 4.65. Management referenced two recent fatalities in the broader east‑coast mining sector, underscoring the seriousness of the safety challenge.

New Acland Quarterly Sales Impacted by Rail

New Acland’s quarterly coal sales slipped to 0.9 million tonnes, down 7% from the prior period. The decline was mainly due to rail cancellations across the network caused by protected industrial action at Queensland Rail, highlighting exposure to external logistics constraints.

Rail Path Constraints Weigh on Performance

Fourth‑quarter rail performance was hampered by industrial action at Queensland Rail and outages linked to the Cross River Rail project. These issues reduced available rail paths, constraining coal movements and limiting the ability to fully realize production gains in sales.

Bengalla Quarterly Unit Cost Volatility

Bengalla’s unit costs shifted from $84 per tonne in the first half to $74 in the third quarter and $84.50 in the fourth. Management attributed the higher fourth‑quarter rate to lower‑than‑planned sales, heavy waste movement following FY2025 weather and broader inflationary pressures.

Inflationary Pressures and Cost Control

Management said the company has been working to stay ahead of cost inflation seen across the industry over the past six months. Efforts are focused on tightening full‑year costs, with an emphasis on productivity and disciplined procurement to protect margins.

Cash Holdings Above Long-Term Target

Current cash balances sit higher than the level management ultimately wants to hold, though they plan to retain more cash than historically. The stance reflects a desire to mitigate funding and site‑stoppage risks, while still allowing room for shareholder returns and project funding.

Worker Contract Negotiations Ahead

A new contract for workers is expected to be finalized later this year. While details were not disclosed, the pending negotiations introduce another operational variable, particularly against a backdrop of industry‑wide inflation and labour‑market tension.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Operational Outlook

Management confirmed New Acland’s ramp‑up toward 5 million tonnes per annum, with Manning Vale West access on track for the second half of 2026 and first coal shortly thereafter. Bengalla’s strip ratio is expected to remain in the 4s on average, with Acland also around 4, and Bengalla’s FY2026 FOB cash cost of $81.30 per tonne landed at the bottom of the guidance range, reinforcing confidence in ongoing cost discipline.

New Hope’s earnings call painted a picture of a miner in strong financial health, leveraging favourable coal markets while investing in organic growth. Record cash flows, production beats and cost control at Bengalla and New Acland were offset by safety concerns, rail constraints and inflation, leaving investors with a constructive yet risk‑aware outlook on the company’s next phase.

data.description:
Growthpoint Properties ((GWWTF)) has held its Q4 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Growthpoint Properties’ latest earnings call struck a cautiously upbeat tone, with management highlighting stronger cash generation, a healthier balance sheet and standout performance from key South African assets, especially the V&A Waterfront. Yet, despite these positives, executives warned that growth is likely to slow, pointing to weak Gauteng offices, pressure in Australia and higher funding costs.

Higher Distributable Income and Dividend

Distributable income per share rose 4.3% to 152.6 cents, giving shareholders another year of real growth. The board boosted the dividend by 7.4%, helped by lifting the payout ratio from 85% to 87.5%, signaling confidence in current cash flows even as future growth is guided lower.

Promotion

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Stronger Balance Sheet and Capital Capacity

Growthpoint’s balance sheet ended the year in better shape, with group loan-to-value easing to 38.7% and assets up 2.8% to ZAR 160 billion. Net asset value per share climbed 3.8%, while South Africa’s LTV dropped to 30.2%, supported by ZAR 5.7 billion in undrawn facilities and over ZAR 300 million in cash.

Successful Debt Issuance and Refinancing

The group’s debt market access remained robust, issuing ZAR 1.8 billion of bonds at 108 basis points over ZARONIA across three to seven years. Demand was strong, with the book six times oversubscribed, and subsequent private placements of ZAR 3.1 billion included a notable 10-year tranche, locking in long-term funding.

Portfolio Repositioning Through Disposals and Reinvestment

Management continued reshaping the portfolio, selling 29 assets worth ZAR 4.9 billion, predominantly offices and logistics. At the same time, the group invested ZAR 1.3 billion in developments and committed a further ZAR 3.6 billion, heavily tilted toward logistics, industrial and retail rather than traditional office space.

Long-Term Portfolio Transformation

Over the past decade, Growthpoint has sold nearly ZAR 20 billion of properties, reducing its asset count from 471 to 302. Office exposure fell from 46% of portfolio value in 2015 to 39%, while industrial grew from 15% to 20%, reflecting a deliberate shift toward more resilient sectors.

Strong South African Portfolio Performance

South African operations delivered solid underlying growth, with like-for-like net property income up 4.4%. The group renewed close to one million square metres of space, cut vacancies from 8.2% to 7.2% and achieved renewal success above 80%, supported by average rental escalations of 6.8%.

South African Property Valuation Growth

Domestic property valuations rose 3.3%, adding ZAR 2 billion in value largely thanks to higher income rather than richer valuation multiples. Industrial assets led with 6.4% growth, followed by offices at 2.9% and retail at 2.1%, underlining the relative strength of income-generating fundamentals.

Retail Portfolio Shows Positive Momentum

Retail remained a bright spot, with trading densities increasing 2.7% and annualized sales per square metre above ZAR 37,000. Renewal success exceeded 90%, vacancies sat at a low 3.5% and rental reversions turned slightly positive, supported by escalations north of 6%.

Industrial and Logistics Portfolio Growth

Logistics assets posted like-for-like growth of 4.9%, with vacancies below 3% and renewal success around 80%. Escalations for in-force and renewed leases were strong at roughly 7.3% to 7.4%, and a 38,000-square-metre development at Montague Gardens has already been fully pre-let ahead of its 2027 completion.

Western Cape Office Recovery

Western Cape offices showed clear signs of recovery, with positive rental reversion of 0.4% and vacancies outside the V&A Waterfront falling to 3.6%. Broader provincial office vacancies are below 4%, and new leases are achieving escalations above 7%, contrasting sharply with challenged Gauteng markets.

V&A Waterfront Delivers Exceptional Results

The V&A Waterfront again stood out, lifting its distribution to ZAR 965 million from ZAR 810 million and growing net property income by 21%. Even stripping out residential apartment sales, underlying NPI growth was high single to low double digits, with visitor numbers up 7% and vacancies around 1%.

V&A Waterfront Development and Sector Growth

The precinct secured an extra 440,000 square metres of development rights, reinforcing its long-term growth runway. Income across marine, industrial, office and retail segments grew strongly, while hospitality still edged higher despite the temporary closure and redevelopment of The Table Bay hotel.

GOZ Operational Performance Remains Positive

In Australia, Growthpoint’s platform delivered modest growth, with FFO per share up 0.9% and the core dividend up 1.1%. Properties remained well occupied at 96%, WALE was a healthy six years, and the business completed a record year of leasing in both office and industrial despite macro headwinds.

Globalworth Maintains Strong Operating Metrics

Globalworth’s operating engine held up, with net operating income rising 0.6% and revenue improving slightly. Vacancies edged down to 13.4%, cash balances were robust at over EUR 270 million and LTV fell to 36.7%, supported by bond repayments and extensive interest-rate hedging.

Growthpoint Investment Partners Expansion

The investment partners arm continued to scale, with healthcare fund fees climbing from ZAR 46 million to ZAR 56 million. The Auria deal pushed the fund into life rights and aged care, while the student accommodation vehicle expanded with a 2,400-bed project scheduled for completion in time for the 2027 student intake.

Renewable Energy and ESG Progress

Growthpoint is stepping up its energy transition, having invested over ZAR 1 billion in 98 solar plants with 69 MW peak capacity. Renewable penetration rose to 19% from 7.9%, while the group maintained a top-tier BEE score and continued sizable spending on corporate social responsibility and education.

Long-Term Shareholder Return Track Record

Management highlighted the group’s long-run record under CEO Norbert Sasse, with market capitalization climbing from about ZAR 3.7 billion to ZAR 57 billion. Over more than two decades, total shareholder returns have consistently exceeded 12% annually, reinforcing the company’s track record as a compounding vehicle.

FY2027 Growth Guidance Moderates

Looking ahead, Growthpoint expects FY2027 distributable income and dividends to grow only 1% to 3%. With the payout ratio held at 87.5%, management sees around 1.3% growth in both DIPS and dividends, reflecting more cautious assumptions on interest rates and asset disposals.

South African Office Reversions Remain Negative

Despite broader portfolio strength, South African offices remain a drag, with overall lease renewal reversion at -2.3%. Office rentals fell more sharply, with reversions of -6.3% nationwide and -10.2% in Gauteng, where vacancies sit at a high 18.6% in pockets like Midrand and Parktown.

Gauteng Office Market Underperformance

Management described Gauteng offices as the primary headwind for South African performance and noted the weakness predates COVID. Limited municipal infrastructure investment and sluggish regional economic growth continue to weigh on demand, making this market structurally more challenging.

Industrial Portfolio Had Slightly Negative Reversion

Industrial and logistics recorded marginally negative rental reversion of -0.5%, though management stressed this was confined to non-core assets. In many of these properties, rents were deliberately trimmed to keep occupancy high while buildings are prepared for eventual sale.

Disposals Expected to Reduce Near-Term NPI

The disposal program is reshaping the portfolio but is near-term dilutive, with roughly ZAR 7.5 billion of assets sold over two years. Because reinvestment is lagging sales, management expects absolute net property income to decline next year, even if like-for-like metrics remain healthy.

Australian Interest-Rate and Property-Market Pressure

Australia’s macro backdrop remains tough, with interest rates at 15-year highs and risk of another hike. This environment is curbing economic activity and weighing on both listed and direct property values, adding pressure to Growthpoint’s Australian segment despite solid operational performance.

GOZ Leverage and Valuation Decline

GOZ’s leverage sits just above the preferred ceiling, with LTV around 41%, and asset values declined modestly during the year. NTA per share fell 1.3%, mainly due to softer valuations in office and industrial portfolios, as yields expanded and investor caution increased.

High Australian Leasing Incentives and Melbourne Challenges

To win and retain tenants, GOZ is offering leasing incentives of 30% to 50%, with the highest levels in Melbourne. Management highlighted Melbourne’s office market as particularly difficult, citing elevated vacancies and a local policy environment seen as unfriendly to investors.

GOZ Funds-Management Assets Under Management Declined

The Australian funds-management business saw assets under management shrink from AUD 1.4 billion to AUD 1.2 billion. The decline reflected AUD 331 million returned to investors as funds matured, partially offset by AUD 125 million of new assets, indicating a net outflow as cycles rolled off.

Lower Offshore Income

Offshore income fell sharply when translated into rand, dropping nearly ZAR 300 million to ZAR 1.1 billion. The decline was driven by disposals of UK retail stakes, a stronger rand and reduced dividends from Globalworth, tempering the contribution from international operations.

Globalworth Dividend Decline and Long-Term Underperformance

Globalworth cut its dividend per share from EUR 0.14 to EUR 0.12, citing discount impacts from its reinvestment plan, higher financing costs and extra Polish taxes. Management openly acknowledged that this minority stake has underperformed for a prolonged period within the offshore book.

Lango Portfolio Valuation Write-Down

Growthpoint’s African exposure via Lango also faced pressure, with portfolio valuations declining 3.7% to USD 788 million. The group’s 18.9% stake is now valued at USD 633 million, reflecting broader valuation headwinds across the region’s commercial property markets.

Healthcare Fund Dividend Decline and Higher Reported LTV

Dividends from the healthcare fund dropped to ZAR 71 million from ZAR 90 million, mainly due to debt-funded expansion through the Auria acquisition. Reported LTV rose to 51%, though management emphasized that excluding life-rights liabilities, leverage would sit at a much lower 29%.

Higher Funding Costs and Interest-Rate Assumptions

The group expects South African interest rates to remain elevated and has built in two further hikes into its forecasts. In Australia, cross-currency swaps that previously cost just over 2% were refinanced at just over 4%, effectively doubling related interest expenses and squeezing margins.

Waterfront Infrastructure and Densification Challenges

At the V&A Waterfront, management stressed the need to balance new development with infrastructure renewal and public-space preservation. Major water-reticulation upgrades and related roadworks are underway, temporarily narrowing routes and highlighting the cost of maintaining a 25-year-old precinct.

Moderated Outlook and FY2027 Guidance

For FY2027, Growthpoint is guiding to low single-digit growth, with dividends and distributable income expected to rise 1% to 3%. The group anticipates lower absolute NPI due to ongoing disposals of ZAR 2 billion to ZAR 3 billion annually, while interest rates are assumed to stay high, dampening overall momentum.

In closing, Growthpoint’s earnings call painted a picture of a company in solid financial health, steadily reshaping its portfolio and leaning on strong assets like the V&A Waterfront and Western Cape offices. However, investors should brace for slower growth as disposals, high interest rates and weak Gauteng offices weigh on the near-term outlook, even as long-term fundamentals remain resilient.

These gains were presented as evidence that strategic changes are working, even as declining sales, a soft U.K. consumer, and expected second-half pressures temper the outlook.

Quarterly Earnings Significantly Improved

Genesco reported a much smaller adjusted operating loss than a year ago, beating internal expectations across all businesses. Second-quarter adjusted operating loss narrowed to $8 million from $14 million, while adjusted diluted loss per share improved to $0.83 from $1.14, underscoring solid progress on profitability.

Gross Margin Expansion and Expense Discipline

At the same time, adjusted operating expenses fell by about $6 million year over year, showing tighter cost control even as the company invests in growth initiatives.

Journeys Delivered Eighth Consecutive Positive Comp

Journeys remained a clear bright spot with its eighth straight quarter of positive comparable sales, across both stores and e-commerce. Comparable sales at the banner rose 2% in the quarter, reinforcing Journeys’ position as Genesco’s primary growth engine in a mixed retail environment.

Journeys Product Momentum and Full-Price Selling

Product strength at Journeys was broad-based, spanning athletic, casual, lifestyle running, sandals, and fashion-forward silhouettes like Mary Janes and sneaker ballerinas. Management noted larger transaction sizes, higher conversion, and more full-price selling across more than eight brands, pointing to healthier demand and pricing power.

Journeys 4.0 Format Expansion

The upgraded Journeys 4.0 store format continued to deliver sales lifts exceeding 25% versus legacy stores. Genesco opened 25 new locations in the quarter and now targets 95 4.0 stores for the year, which would bring the format to roughly 180 stores, or about 20% of the total fleet, by year-end.

Journeys Expense Leverage and Store Productivity

Journeys generated 180 basis points of expense leverage, reflecting rising productivity in the 4.0 stores and ongoing fleet optimization. Cost-reduction moves and selling-salary efficiencies contributed to the improvement, helping translate sales gains into better bottom-line performance.

Journeys Back-to-School Acceleration

Back-to-school season provided an extra boost, with Journeys’ August comparable sales rising mid-single digits despite a tough two-year comparison. Trends were supported by the Life on Loud marketing campaign and tax-free shopping periods, which helped drive timely traffic and purchases.

Journeys Brand-Building Campaign Traction

Genesco ramped Journeys’ media spending by more than 30% and is seeing payback in engagement and traffic. The Life on Loud campaign generated over 260 million impressions in its first four weeks, while TikTok and Instagram engagement rose 30%, translating into increased visits to stores and journeys.com.

Journeys Store Consolidation Performance

The company is also testing larger, consolidated formats that combine Journeys and Journeys Kid locations. A revamped San Antonio store delivered sales up more than 70% month-to-date, well ahead of target, and Genesco opened its first 4.0 Journeys Kids store in Texas with seven more planned this year.

Johnston & Murphy Continued Positive Momentum

Johnston & Murphy posted its third straight quarter of positive comps, with sales up 4% on improved assortments and pricing. Enhanced brand marketing, stronger traffic, and better conversion helped the banner outpace industry trends, reinforcing its role as a premium growth driver.

Johnston & Murphy Profit and Customer Growth

Profit at Johnston & Murphy improved as both sales and margins moved higher, supported by double-digit growth from new customers. The brand has seen revenue from new buyers climb for 10 consecutive months under the Peyton Manning campaign, with apparel up double digits and footwear growth led by casual and casual athletic styles.

Peyton Manning Partnership Extended

Genesco extended its partnership with Peyton Manning for another two years to sustain Johnston & Murphy’s marketing momentum. Management cited Manning’s high recognition with the target customer base, and noted the new campaign launched September 1, one month earlier than last year to capture more fall demand.

Schuh Gross Margin and Operating Income Progress

Schuh’s sales fell, but profitability showed improvement as gross margin expanded by 300 basis points. A 10-point increase in full-price mix and cost-structure initiatives helped drive nearly flat operating income despite lower revenue, signaling early traction in the chain’s reset strategy.

Schuh Product Access and Leadership

The U.K. banner is elevating its assortment, gaining better access to key brands like adidas, Nike, ASICS, UGG, New Balance, and Birkenstock. Leadership is also evolving, with Tomas Petersson appointed president following Colin Temple’s retirement, as Genesco seeks to sharpen Schuh’s positioning.

Structural Cost-Savings Program

Genesco detailed a multi-year structural savings plan aimed at boosting profitability and funding investments. The company expects up to $20 million of savings in fiscal 2027 from productivity, operational efficiencies, procurement, and AI and automation, with another $20 million to $30 million anticipated over the following two years.

Tariff Refunds Received

During the quarter, Genesco received roughly $22 million in tariff refunds tied to branded businesses that import product. These refunds, representing about 20% of the company, were excluded from adjusted results, signaling management’s focus on underlying operating performance.

Share Repurchases and Liquidity

Genesco continued returning capital by repurchasing about 318,000 shares, roughly 3% of its outstanding stock, for $11 million through August 31. With $19 million remaining under its authorization, management emphasized a healthy balance sheet, strong liquidity, and expected solid cash generation in the second half.

Raised Full-Year Earnings Outlook

Despite revenue pressure, the company raised its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to the high end of the $2.00 to $2.40 range. Guidance now calls for 60 to 80 basis points of gross margin expansion and adjusted operating income still between $34 million and $40 million, with the top end now seen as most likely.

Quarterly Revenue and Comparable Sales Declined

Top-line trends were weaker, with second-quarter revenue down 3% to $530 million and comparable sales off 1%. Genesco ended the quarter with 67 fewer net stores than a year ago, reducing fleet and square footage by around 5%, but only trimming about 2% of sales as it prunes underperforming locations.

Schuh Comparable Sales Decline

Comparable sales at Schuh fell 9%, largely due to a deliberate cutback in promotions amid a deeply promotional U.K. footwear market. Management said the U.K. consumer remains challenged and price sensitive, adding pressure as Schuh prioritizes margin health over near-term volume.

E-Commerce Comparable Sales Decline

Company-wide e-commerce comps slipped 6%, with Schuh’s reduced discounting weighing heavily on online results. Johnston & Murphy’s digital performance also cooled as a pullback in catalog activity disproportionately affected that banner’s web channel during the quarter.

Sales Headwinds from Strategic Actions

Management stressed that several sales headwinds are self-inflicted and tied to long-term strategic moves. Store closures, license transitions ahead of the Wrangler launch, and the shift away from heavy discounting at Schuh are suppressing near-term revenue while aiming to build a healthier business model.

Consumer Environment Remains Challenged

Executives described the consumer as selective and intentional, shopping only when there is a clear reason. They expect choppy behavior for the rest of the year, with softer comparable sales during non-peak periods as shoppers remain cautious about discretionary spending.

More Promotional Activity Expected in Athletic

Genesco anticipates increased promotional intensity in athletic footwear and certain apparel categories in the second half. The company intends to stay disciplined on price and maintain a focus on full-price selling, even as competitive pressures rise in those segments.

Schuh Turnaround Still Incomplete

Management acknowledged that Schuh’s turnaround remains a work in progress and will take longer than the Journeys reset. While product elevation is advancing, the positive impact is being masked by lower sales tied to the promotion pullback, delaying clear evidence of the banner’s recovery.

Lower Second-Half Sales Outlook

Reflecting Schuh’s added pressure, Genesco trimmed its full-year sales expectations. Comparable sales are now forecast to be flat versus a prior outlook of up 1% to 2%, and total sales are expected to be down about 2% compared with a previous view ranging from down 1% to flat.

Third-Quarter Sales and Operating Income Pressure

For the third quarter, the company expects total sales to decline slightly more than 4% to 4.5%, including a $14 million hit from license exits and store closures. Operating income is projected to be moderately below last year, as SG&A deleverage more than offsets 90 to 100 basis points of anticipated gross-margin expansion.

Third-Quarter Investment-Related SG&A Pressure

Third-quarter SG&A is also being lifted by growth investments, including heavier back-to-school marketing and the expanded Peyton Manning campaign. These pressures, totaling about 100 basis points, will add to the impact of lower sales but are aimed at strengthening brand equity and future earnings power.

Tax Rate Reduced Second-Quarter EPS Benefit

Management noted that the quarter’s adjusted loss per share understated operating progress due to a much lower tax rate. A valuation allowance discussed previously drove the change, meaning the EPS figure does not fully reflect the underlying improvement in operating income.

Tariff Exposure Remains Under Review

Genesco continues to manage tariff risk through pricing, sourcing, and mix adjustments while monitoring potential exposure from new trade actions. Importantly, the company’s adjusted outlook assumes no future benefit from additional tariff refunds, keeping guidance conservative on this front.

Seasonal and Weather-Related Uncertainty

The company highlighted seasonal uncertainty, noting persistent hot weather has delayed the boot-selling season. Management said cooler fall temperatures will be needed for consumers to shift into fall footwear, adding another variable to second-half performance.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Outlook

Genesco now expects fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS to land at the high end of its $2.00 to $2.40 range, supported by up to $20 million in structural savings. Full-year comparable sales are projected to be flat, total sales down about 2%, gross margin up 60 to 80 basis points, and SG&A deleveraging about 30 basis points, with operating income likely near the top of the $34 million to $40 million band.

Genesco’s call painted a picture of a retailer successfully reshaping its portfolio while navigating a tough consumer backdrop. Profitability and margin gains at Journeys, Johnston & Murphy, and Schuh are encouraging, even as sales trends and U.K. weakness pose challenges. For investors, the story is one of disciplined execution, selective growth investment, and a cautiously optimistic earnings outlook.

TEN has taken delivery of seven vessels from its 26-ship newbuilding program, and management reports valuations have risen by at least 30%. The roughly $3.1 billion program has appreciated by at least that amount even before full delivery, underscoring the market value of modern tonnage.

Modernized and Expanded Fleet Profile

Since early 2023, TEN sold 20 older vessels averaging 17.3 years and 2 million deadweight tons, replacing them with 35 modern ships averaging 0.5 years and 4.8 million deadweight tons. The pro forma fleet now totals 81 vessels, including LNG units and a sizable 16-vessel shuttle tanker fleet.

Long-Term Shuttle Tanker Contract

The DP shuttle tanker Anfield has commenced a 10-year charter with a major U.S. oil company, with options extending up to its 20th year. Assuming maximum employment, the vessel’s gross revenue is expected to approach $500 million, adding a long-duration cash flow stream.

High Secured-Revenue Coverage

Of the 62-vessel operating fleet, 23 ships, or 37%, have market exposure via spot or profit-sharing deals, offering upside in strong markets. Meanwhile, 52 vessels, or 84%, are in secured revenue arrangements, balancing earnings stability with selective leverage to spot rates.

Solid Balance Sheet and Cash Position

TEN’s pro forma fleet carries an estimated fair market value of $4.9 billion against $2 billion of debt, implying net debt-to-capital of about 44.5%. Cash at June 30, 2026 stood at $466 million, up $179 million year on year and $168 million from year-end 2025, strengthening liquidity.

Asset Sales Unlocking Value

The company sold two 2006-built Suezmax tankers to third parties for net proceeds of $100 million after repurchasing them at a discount. The transaction highlights TEN’s ability to capture embedded value in older assets while reallocating capital toward newer, higher-earning vessels.

Dividend Growth and Shareholder Rewards

TEN has paid $0.60 and $1.00 per share in dividends during 2026, totaling $1.60, and management aims to materially increase shareholder rewards. A new dividend plan is expected after a November strategy meeting, subject to board decisions and prevailing market conditions.

Preferred Share Redemption Opportunity

Management is weighing the use of cash to redeem $120 million of perpetual preferred shares carrying a 9.25% coupon. Retiring this high-cost capital could boost annual EPS by an estimated $0.30 to $0.40 through interest savings, further enhancing equity returns.

Positive Market and Revenue Outlook

The company expects 2026 revenue to significantly exceed $1 billion, with an even stronger second half than the already profitable first half. Management also sees at least good and growing prospects into next year, supported by firm tanker markets and its modern fleet.

Operational Upside from Spot Exposure

Through profit-sharing arrangements, TEN estimates that every $1,000 per day increase in spot rates adds $0.11 to annual EPS, based on 23 vessels currently exposed. This sensitivity provides a clear metric for investors tracking tanker market movements and potential earnings upside.

Severe Geopolitical and Security Risks

Management described a turbulent geopolitical backdrop, including conflict in the Middle East, regional disruptions and attacks on oceangoing vessels. These events have created serious risks for crews and ships, reinforcing the need for careful route planning and risk management.

Operational Avoidance of High-Risk Routes

TEN continues to avoid transits through the Strait of Hormuz due to attacks, disruptions and unsafe conditions in the area. Executives characterized the environment as an operational minefield, with decisions centered on protecting crews, vessels and the environment.

Higher Bunker and Voyage Expenses

First-half voyage expenses increased to about $82 million from $68 million, mainly due to a roughly 25% rise in bunker prices for spot-trading vessels. Second-quarter voyage costs climbed to $52 million from $32 million, partially offsetting the benefits of higher freight rates.

Rising Operating and Administrative Costs

Vessel operating expenses rose to $111 million from $102 million, reflecting a slightly larger fleet, more dry-dock work and inflation. Depreciation and amortization increased to $90 million from $83 million, while general and administrative costs edged up to $27 million from $23 million.

Increased Debt from Fleet Expansion

Financial obligations associated with fleet growth expanded to $2.1 billion at the end of June 2026, compared with $1.8 billion a year earlier. While leverage has risen, it is anchored by higher asset values and contracted earnings, though it adds to TEN’s financial risk profile.

Dry-Dock Activity and Maintenance

Six ships underwent scheduled dry-dock in the first half of 2026 versus five a year earlier, and four were in dock in the second quarter compared with three. This elevated maintenance activity temporarily reduces earning days but supports long-term operational reliability.

Oil Prices and Global Demand Dynamics

Management noted that conflict in the Middle East and route disruptions have lifted crude and product prices, dampening global oil demand. At the same time, these geopolitical shifts have tightened tanker supply-demand balances, contributing to stronger freight markets.

Fleet Carve-Out Plans on the Back Burner

A potential carve-out of roughly 20 long-term-chartered vessels is not viewed as a near-term priority by management. Any such deal would remain within TEN and is currently described as only exploratory, with no imminent transaction expected.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Growth Plans

Looking ahead, TEN expects 2026 revenues to significantly exceed $1 billion alongside very strong EBITDA and a major second-half profit-sharing uplift. The company plans to maintain semi-annual dividends, aims to increase payouts after its November strategy review, will take delivery of 19 newbuilds and sees good and growing prospects over at least the next year.

Tsakos Energy Navigation’s earnings call painted the picture of a company in a powerful upcycle, combining record financial results with a modern, expanding fleet and visible long-term revenues. While geopolitical risk, higher costs and larger debt loads remain concerns, management’s confident outlook and plans to enhance shareholder returns make TEN a name to watch in the tanker space.

Since the previous call, Coda secured about $1.4 million of U.S. Navy orders for DAVID tethered systems and peripherals, including four DAVID Flex units and Echoscope sonars for training. The firm is working with subsea robotic OEMs, research organizations, and direct customers worldwide, with growing interest from U.S. and European defense markets and various underwater systems.

The initial order covers three systems on the vehicle, and management sees additional customer opportunities if these trials deliver strong results.

Strategic Investment in Next‑Gen Tech and VoiceHub 4

The company is also future‑proofing Echoscope for more underwater platforms and advancing VoiceHub 4 after redesigning it to lower bill‑of‑materials costs.

Retained Earnings Milestone and Active M&A Pipeline

The company moved from an accumulated deficit to positive retained earnings for the first time, reflecting sustained profitability and financial discipline. Coda also remains actively engaged in evaluating acquisitions that fit its strategic goals, hinting at potential deal‑driven expansion.

Marine Technology Hit by Geopolitics and Hardware Drop

Marine technology revenue fell 15.2% to $3.4 million from $4.0 million, mainly due to geopolitical instability in the Middle East and parts of Asia limiting customer activity. Within that segment, hardware revenue declined 17.8% to $2.3 million from $2.7 million, underscoring the impact of regional disruptions.

Deferral of Marine Opportunities Amid Regional Uncertainty

Management said ongoing uncertainty has caused security concerns, offshore project disruptions, and supply‑chain issues for end customers in affected regions. While these factors are leading to deferred orders, the company does not believe the situation reflects structural weakness in the underlying marine technology market.

Compressed Consolidated and Segment Margins

Consolidated gross margin slipped to 65.4% from 68.3%, driven by shifts in revenue composition, geography, and project mix. Acoustic sensors and materials margins eased to 52.4% from 54.8%, while defense engineering services margins fell to 56.9% from 58.9%, both reflecting contract and product mix dynamics.

Defense Revenue Remains Lumpy and Long Cycle

Management cautioned that defense engineering revenue will stay lumpy because sustainment spending depends on annual program budgets and timing of spare‑parts replenishment. They stressed that DAVID, Nano, and related defense opportunities are inherently long‑term, with broader procurement hinging on deployment, user testing, and complex customer processes.

Operating Expenses and Taxes Edge Higher

Total operating expenses rose to $3.5 million from $3.4 million, reflecting greater investment to support growth, while the income tax provision increased to $400,000 from $300,000. Even with these higher charges, Coda maintained year‑over‑year gains in operating income and net earnings.

Forward‑Looking Outlook and Program Milestones

Looking ahead, management expects marine technology activity in Asia and the Middle East to remain affected by deferred opportunities but views this as temporary rather than structural. Defense sustainment revenue will stay uneven, SAT trials for an underwater ROV program are expected to conclude in the fourth quarter, visibility into a European Navy’s procurement roadmap should improve later this fiscal year, and R&D and SG&A spending are set to increase as Coda pursues longer‑term defense programs.

Coda Octopus Group’s earnings call painted a picture of a company leaning into growth in defense and acoustic technologies while absorbing near‑term marine market headwinds and margin pressure. For investors, the combination of rising profitability, a debt‑free balance sheet, and a growing portfolio of longer‑cycle defense programs suggests a business with solid resilience and meaningful optionality, even if revenue streams remain uneven from quarter to quarter.

EBITDA in Business Services increased 18% year-on-year to EUR 8.6 million, pushing the margin up to 21% from 19.9%. Software and System Integration Profitability Trends

EBITDA in Software and System Integration declined 2.5% to EUR 23 million and reported adjusted EAT dipped 1%, though excluding asset disposals, EBITDA was flat and adjusted EAT grew 1%. Management expects this segment to return to revenue growth from Q2 FY 2027, particularly in higher-value technology and integration services.

Growth in Adjusted and Reported Earnings

At group level, adjusted EBIT reached EUR 50.2 million, up 6.2% year-on-year, while reported EBIT climbed 7.5% to EUR 41.4 million. Adjusted EAT rose 7.1% to EUR 30.1 million, underpinned by strong profitability in ICT VAS, Green VAS and Business Services, reinforcing the earnings power of SeSa’s diversified portfolio.

Net Financial Expenses and Cost of Capital

Net financial expenses were around EUR 7.5 million, improving 11% versus the fourth quarter of FY 2026 and in line with the industrial plan assumptions. Strong Cash Generation and Financial Position

Reported net financial position as of July 2026 showed EUR 23.4 million of net debt, an improvement of about EUR 40 million year-on-year despite EUR 120 million of investments and EUR 40 million returned via dividends and buybacks. Excluding IFRS liabilities, SeSa held around EUR 150 million of net cash, slightly better than a year before.

Consistent Operating and Free Cash Flow

Management highlighted that operating cash flow over the last 12 months was about EUR 200 million for the fourth consecutive quarter. Free cash flow over the same period reached roughly EUR 80 million, underscoring SeSa’s ability to fund growth, shareholder returns and acquisitions without stretching its balance sheet.

Sustainability and Information Security Progress

The group continues to extend certifications and increase renewable energy use, integrating sustainability and information security into its long-term strategy.

Stable Workforce and Focus on High-Demand Skills

The workforce remained stable at around 6,700–6,770 people, up roughly 2.5% to 2.7% year-on-year but flat versus April 2026. Management tied this stability to initiatives around skills development, knowledge sharing, AI and automation, efficiency, education, welfare, inclusion and work-life balance, aimed at keeping talent aligned with growth areas.

Higher Dividend and Share Buyback Programs

The new industrial plan confirms a payout ratio of about 40%, and the dividend to be paid in late September will rise from EUR 1 to EUR 1.33 per share. Management sees potential to reach up to EUR 2 per share over the next two years, alongside a EUR 5 million buyback, an additional EUR 5 million program and possible further purchases within a broader authorization.

Positive Market and Order Environment

Management described the Italian digital market as supportive, with expected growth of around 3.5% per year through 2029 driven by AI, cloud, cybersecurity and data management. SeSa continues to grow at roughly twice the market rate and reported a positive order trend, strong ICT VAS momentum and an anticipated recovery in Software and System Integration.

Simplified Holding Structure and Ownership Increase

The merger of two holding entities into the new SeSa Holding was presented as a strategic simplification that clarifies SeSa Holding as the group’s long-term owner. SeSa Holding’s stake has risen to about 57.1% from 52.8% 18 months ago, and management intends to continue increasing its ownership over time.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Outlook

Looking ahead to FY 2027, SeSa confirmed guidance for revenue growth of 5% to 7.5%, targeting EUR 3.8 billion to EUR 3.9 billion. EBITDA is expected to grow 5% to 10% to EUR 274 million–287 million, with adjusted group EAT seen rising 7.5% to 12.5% to EUR 115 million–119 million, driven by continued outperformance versus the Italian digital market.

Green VAS is expected to sustain a 6% EBITDA margin and about 3.5% net profitability, while the company plans to keep growing at roughly twice the national digital market rate.
